title: Relational Database Design & SQL Development
description: I have used relational databases throughout my career for educational platforms, customer-support systems, knowledge bases, business applications, reporting tools and internal administration. My work has included schema design, CRUD, joins, indexes, views, constraints, stored procedures, reporting, schema evolution and custom entity/data-access layers across DB2, SQL Server, MySQL, Aurora MySQL, Access, Derby and SQLite. I generally used explicit SQL and application entities rather than ORMs, and chose relational or NoSQL persistence according to the operational needs of each system.

sections.title: SQL Foundations
paragraphs: I first learned SQL using DB2 while studying computer programming in college, working against DB2 from AIX.
That foundation carried into professional Java, .NET, web and cloud applications using several relational database platforms.

sections.title: Early Essential Skills SQL Systems
paragraphs: Essential Skills maintained SQL Server internally during our years as a Microsoft Partner, and I used relational databases for several early internal systems.
items: Java / SQL Server customer-service and technical-support tracking

sections.title: Public Business Applications
paragraphs: My first substantial production-facing SQL web application was the Essential Skills ASP.NET business website and ordering system.
I built the application in C#/ASP.NET using ADO.NET with SQL Server for the product catalog, customer/order workflow and administrative data.

sections.title: VB.NET / Access Application
paragraphs: I also developed a public-facing funeral-home application using VB.NET and Microsoft Access.
Access was otherwise used primarily for smaller applications, internal tools and persistence experiments rather than as the main database for the later Essential Skills production platform.

sections.title: Schema & Data Modeling
paragraphs: I designed the relational schemas used by my applications rather than treating the database as an externally supplied black box.

sections.title: Practical SQL Workloads
paragraphs: Most of the systems I built had straightforward business and educational data relationships, so the SQL emphasized maintainable application queries rather than unnecessarily complex database logic.

sections.title: CRUD, Reporting & Joins
paragraphs: My day-to-day relational work was primarily CRUD, reporting, joins and schema design.
The application domains generally required only a small number of understandable joins rather than highly specialized analytical SQL.

sections.title: Stored Procedures
paragraphs: Where several database operations needed to be grouped into one controlled operation, I used stored procedures to encapsulate the chained calls.
I learned and experimented with T-SQL but did not build the production architecture around extensive T-SQL-specific programming.

sections.title: Explicit Data Access
paragraphs: I generally did not use ORMs.
Application data was commonly loaded into Java- or application-style entity objects, with explicit persistence classes responsible for converting between those entities and the underlying database.

sections.title: Database Connectivity
paragraphs: I worked through multiple database-access technologies as application stacks changed over time.

sections.title: SmartDB / Rosetta Integration
paragraphs: SQL databases later became interchangeable persistence plugins behind the Hydra-Gen SmartDB/Rosetta architecture.
This allowed the business layer to work with common application entities while individual adapters handled differences between SQL and non-SQL storage engines.

sections.title: Proof of Portability
paragraphs: I implemented Access and SQLite SmartDB adapters partly as proof-of-concept backends to demonstrate that the abstraction was not tied to one database vendor.
Apache Derby was also supported; I believe another member of the SmartDB team implemented that plugin.

sections.title: MySQL
paragraphs: I used MySQL in several contexts, including my earlier personal portfolio and later production architecture.

sections.title: Amazon Aurora / Version 7
paragraphs: The Essential Skills Version 7 database used Amazon Aurora with MySQL compatibility.
I designed and administered the application database while AWS supplied and managed the underlying Aurora database service.

sections.title: Schema Evolution
paragraphs: Our schemas were generally stable and deliberately kept understandable, so they did not require elaborate migration frameworks.
When tables or fields changed, I kept application versions compatible with the data wherever possible and performed rebuilds or reindexing when necessary.

sections.title: Choosing SQL When It Fit
paragraphs: SQL was an important part of my persistence experience, but I did not treat relational databases as the automatic answer for every system.

As our architecture moved into AWS, I often selected SimpleDB or other cloud-oriented persistence approaches when their deployment simplicity, scaling model and operating cost better matched the application.
